cells.caption: Mecia de Viladestes, portolan chart, 1413
cells.detail: whaling scene in the North Atlantic
cells.interpretation: A whaling scene, rather than evidence that the whale was considered imaginary. The supplied scan is already a detail of the portolan chart.

cells.caption: Martin Waldseemüller, Carta marina, 1516
cells.detail: “Morsus animal ingens quantitate elephantis”
cells.interpretation: The label describes an animal as large as an elephant. “Morsus” is read here as a walrus; the comparison concerns size, not a modern species description.

cells.caption: Olaus Magnus, Carta marina, 1539
cells.detail: “Balena” attacked by “Orcha”
cells.interpretation: Balena means whale; Orcha names its attacker. These are historical labels, not precise modern species identifications.

cells.caption: Olaus Magnus, Carta marina, 1539
cells.detail: “Ros marus piscis”, by “Vardahus”
cells.interpretation: Ros marus piscis is the historical walrus label; Vardahus refers to Vardø. Piscis reflects the source’s classification, not modern mammal taxonomy.

cells.caption: Olaus Magnus, Carta marina, 1539
cells.detail: unnamed horned head; sea-unicorn? (our reading)
cells.interpretation: Tentatively identified here as a sea-unicorn. The horned head has no identifying label; the connection with a narwhal is our interpretation.

cells.caption: Abraham Ortelius, Islandia, 1590
cells.detail: L · Steipereidur
cells.interpretation: L · Steipereidur: a historical Icelandic whale name, associated with the blue whale. The plate preserves the map’s spelling; the picture is not a diagnostic species portrait. Supplied scan: 1983 facsimile of the 1590 map.

cells.caption: Abraham Ortelius, Islandia, 1590
cells.detail: N · Rostunger
cells.interpretation: N · Rostunger: walrus. Supplied scan: 1983 facsimile of Islandia (1590).

cells.caption: Abraham Ortelius, Islandia, 1590
cells.detail: A · Nahval
cells.interpretation: A · Nahval: narwhal. Supplied scan: 1983 facsimile of Islandia (1590).

cells.caption: Thomas Edge, in Purchas His Pilgrimes, 1625
cells.detail: vignette on the “Greneland” map of Spitsbergen
cells.interpretation: A border vignette on a map of Spitsbergen called Greneland. It is included as a map image even though the map appeared in a book.

cells.caption: Hessel Gerritsz, Histoire du pays nommé Spitsberghe, 1613
cells.detail: walrus and calf
cells.interpretation: Walrus and calf in a printed account of Spitsbergen. The comparison does not demonstrate influence on the later examples.

cells.caption: Ole Worm, Museum Wormianum, 1655
cells.detail: “Unicornu marinum”: narwhal and its skull, pp. 282–283
cells.interpretation: Unicornu marinum means marine unicorn. Worm’s narwhal illustration is paired with a skull on the next page; these are two crops in one cell.

cells.caption: William Scoresby, Arctic Regions, 1820, pl. XII
cells.detail: “Balæna Mysticetus, or Common Whale”
cells.interpretation: Balæna Mysticetus, or Common Whale: the bowhead whale, in Scoresby’s 1820 account, plate XII.

cells.caption: John Webber, “Sea Horses”, 1785 printing
cells.detail: Cook’s Voyage first published in 1784
cells.interpretation: Sea Horses means walruses here. This image’s imprint is 1785; Cook’s Voyage was first published in 1784. The plate now distinguishes those dates.

cells.caption: William Scoresby, Arctic Regions, 1820, pl. XV
cells.detail: “Male Narwal, or Unicorn”
cells.interpretation: Male Narwal, or Unicorn: narwhal, Scoresby’s 1820 account, plate XV.

cells.caption: Olaus Magnus, Carta marina, 1539
cells.detail: a serpent coils round a ship off Norway
cells.interpretation: A sea serpent coils around a ship off Norway. Its placement and imagery are documented; the identity of a real animal behind the story is not established here.

cells.caption: Olaus Magnus, Historia, 1555, p. 763
cells.detail: “De Polypis”: a giant crayfish takes a sailor
cells.interpretation: De Polypis means On polyps. The illustration resembles a giant crayfish. It is grouped here with kraken imagery for comparison, not identified as a giant squid.

cells.caption: Hans Egede’s sea serpent, seen 1734
cells.detail: off Greenland; as printed by Pontoppidan, 1753
cells.interpretation: A reported sighting in 1734; the reproduction is attributed to Pontoppidan’s 1753 publication. A reported event date is not the date of this printed image.

cells.caption: Illustrated London News, 28 October 1848
cells.detail: “The sea-serpent when first seen from H.M.S. Dædalus”
cells.interpretation: An engraving published in the Illustrated London News on 28 October 1848. The Library of Congress record confirms the issue date. This is a representation of a reported sighting, not a photograph.

cells.caption: Montfort, Mollusques II, An X (1801–02)
cells.detail: “Le poulpe colossal”, pl. XXVI · Smithsonian scan
cells.interpretation: Le poulpe colossal means the colossal octopus. Montfort distinguished this from his kraken octopus. This is a scan of plate XXVI from the Smithsonian Libraries copy of volume II, original French edition, Paris, F. Dufart, An X (1801–1802). The sheet reads “Pl. XXVI”, “T. 2. P. 256” and “Le poulpe colossal”; the title page verifies the publisher and year. The exact Gregorian publication month remains unknown.

cells.caption: “The great sea-serpent”, Bermuda, 1860
cells.detail: an oarfish; wood engraving after W. D. Munro
cells.interpretation: The print calls the animal a sea-serpent; it is identified here as an oarfish. The reported find was 22 January 1860; the engraving appeared in Harper’s Weekly on 3 March 1860.

cells.caption: The Alecton and the giant squid, 1861
cells.detail: off Tenerife; print after E. Rodolphe, 1865
cells.interpretation: The Alecton encounter took place on 30 November 1861; the supplied print is dated 1865, after E. Rodolphe. The encounter date and image date differ.

cells.caption: Giant squid, Logy Bay, 1873 specimen
cells.detail: photographed 2 December 1873; annotated by A. E. Verrill
cells.interpretation: Caught at Logy Bay in November 1873. Alexander Murray’s contemporary report dates the head-and-arms and body photographs to 2 December 1873, crediting Parsons and McKenna at St. John’s. The report appeared in February 1874; that is its publication date. Harvey later described taking the head and arms in his sponge bath to photographic rooms and suspending them from a crossbar. Verrill’s annotations are distinct from the original photograph.

cells.caption: The Psalter map, c. 1265
cells.detail: two dragons beneath the world
cells.interpretation: Two dragons below the world on the Psalter map. These figures belong to the map’s religious framing; their position is not a mapped animal habitat. The supplied scan is already a detail.

cells.caption: The Hunt–Lenox globe, c. 1510
cells.detail: “HC SVNT DRACONES”, off the coast of Asia
cells.interpretation: HC SVNT DRACONES means Here are dragons. This is lettering on a globe, not a drawing of a dragon. The conventional date is c. 1510; it is approximate.

cells.caption: Ulisse Aldrovandi, Serpentum et draconum historiae, 1640
cells.detail: winged dragons flank the title page
cells.interpretation: Winged dragons frame the title page of a 1640 natural-history book. This is a decorative setting, not a geographical placement.

cells.caption: Ulisse Aldrovandi, Serpentum et draconum historiae, 1640
cells.detail: the seven-headed hydra, p. 387
cells.interpretation: A seven-headed hydra on page 387. Inclusion in a natural-history book does not establish that the depicted animal existed.

cells.caption: Johannes Hevelius, star atlas, 1690
cells.detail: “Draco” coiled round the pole of the ecliptic
cells.interpretation: Draco means dragon. This 1690 star chart illustrates an ancient constellation, already listed by Ptolemy; it is not evidence of dragons moving from earth maps to the sky.

cells.caption: Johannes Hevelius, star atlas, 1690
cells.detail: “Hydra”, with Crater and Corvus on its back
cells.interpretation: Hydra means water snake; Crater (cup) and Corvus (raven) appear beside it. This constellation is ancient, not a 1690 invention.

cells.caption: Albertus Seba, Thesaurus, 1734, pl. CII
cells.detail: fig. 2: a flying lizard, later named Draco
cells.interpretation: A flying lizard, figure 2 on plate CII. Draco is also a later zoological genus name; that does not establish a biological identity for the earlier mythical dragons.

cells.caption: Albertus Seba, Thesaurus, 1734, pl. CII
cells.detail: fig. 1: the Hamburg hydra, a fake
cells.interpretation: The Hamburg hydra, figure 1 on plate CII, is treated here as a fabricated specimen. The cabinet image is a record of a historical claim, not evidence of a living seven-headed animal.
